title: Points of the z-Plane
intro: Each point z of the plane is a test: weight sample n by z to the power −n and see whether the weighted samples add up. Writing z in polar form shows what that weight does: it scales and it turns.

blocks.text: Write a point of the plane in polar form, $z = \rho e^{j\omega}$: $\rho = |z|$ is its distance from the origin and $\omega$ its angle. Then

so the weight on sample $n$ has two parts. The factor $\rho^{-n}$ is a real number that grows or shrinks geometrically with $n$, and $e^{-j\omega n}$ is a unit arrow that turns by $-\omega$ for each step in $n$. Laid out for $n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$, the weights $z^{-n}$ trace a spiral: inward when $\rho > 1$, outward when $\rho < 1$, and round the unit circle when $\rho = 1$.
Substituting into the definition gives the most useful way to read the transform:

For a fixed radius $\rho$, this is the discrete-time Fourier transform of the tilted signal $x[n]\rho^{-n}$. So the z-plane is a stack of circles, and on each circle the z-transform is an ordinary Fourier transform of the signal after it has been multiplied by an exponential $\rho^{-n}$. A larger $\rho$ tames samples at large positive $n$; a smaller $\rho$ tames samples at large negative $n$.
Why some circles work and others don't

Take $x[n] = a^n u[n]$, where $u[n]$ is the unit step (1 for $n \ge 0$, 0 before). On the circle of radius $\rho$ the tilted signal is $(a/\rho)^n u[n]$. Its sum converges exactly when $|a/\rho| < 1$, that is $\rho > |a|$, and then the geometric series gives

Convergence depends only on $|z|$, never on the angle, because the angle only turns the terms. That is why a region of convergence is always made of whole circles: a disc, the outside of a circle, or a ring. The Region of Convergence (#/math/z-transform/region-of-convergence) page follows this up.
A single sample: the plainest surface

The delayed impulse $\delta[n-2]$ is one sample of height 1 at $n = 2$. Its transform has one term, $X(z) = z^{-2}$, so $|X(z)| = 1/|z|^2$: the height depends only on the distance from the origin. The viewer below shows it in plain magnitude: a funnel rising to infinity at $z = 0$ and flattening far away. Written as a rational function, $z^{-2} = 1/z^2$ has a double pole at $z = 0$, and the ROC is every $z$ except $0$. On the unit circle $|z| = 1$ the height is exactly 1 at every frequency, which is what a pure delay should do: it lets every frequency through at full strength and only shifts its phase.

widget.title: A delay seen from the z-plane

blocks.text: Turn the view and watch the red ring: for the delay it lies flat at height 1. Switch Input signal to unit impulse δ[n] and the whole surface is flat at 1, the simplest landscape there is.
A z-transform is a function of position

Two points at the same distance from the origin see the same amount of tilt $\rho^{-n}$ but different turning rates $\omega$. Two points at the same angle see the same turning rate and different tilts. Reading the surface along circles (fixed $\rho$) gives Fourier transforms of tilted signals; reading it along rays (fixed $\omega$) shows how the response to one frequency changes as the signal is tilted.

blocks.title: Weights on a circle
blocks.text: For $z = 0.5 e^{j\pi/2}$, write out the weights $z^{-n}$ for $n = 0, 1, 2, 3$. Which way does the spiral go?
solution: $z^{-1} = 2 e^{-j\pi/2} = -2j$, so the weights are $1, -2j, -4, 8j$: each is twice as long as the one before and turned a quarter-turn clockwise.
With $\rho = 0.5 < 1$, $\rho^{-n} = 2^n$ grows, so the spiral runs outward. A signal that does not shrink faster than $2^{-n}$ will not converge on this circle.

blocks.title: Which circles?
blocks.text: For $x[n] = 3^n u[n]$, on which circles does the z-transform sum converge, and what is $X(z)$ there?
solution: The tilted signal is $(3/\rho)^n u[n]$, which sums when $\rho > 3$. There $X(z) = 1/(1 - 3z^{-1}) = z/(z - 3)$.
